title: SYSK Selects: Can you die of a broken heart?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun (originally aired as an episode on whether a person can die of a broken heart). Josh introduces it as a sweet pick based on an article by Christen Conger. The hosts discuss elderly couples who die together, including a 2010 Milwaukee case of a couple who died by helium asphyxiation in a suicide pact. They explain broken heart syndrome, also called takotsubo cardiomyopathy, a temporary heart condition first identified in Japan in the early 1990s, where stress or grief causes the left ventricle to balloon and mimic a heart attack. They cite a Finnish study showing elevated mortality for surviving spouses after a partner's sudden death, a Scotland/Israel study showing a mortality surge in the first six months of bereavement, brain imaging showing overlapping neural pathways for physical and emotional pain, and a Johns Hopkins study showing very high adrenaline levels in patients. They note takotsubo is more common in women over 55, and debate whether grief truly triggers it. A listener mail follows about Australian bushranger and national hero Ned Kelly, including his homemade armor at Glenrowan, his 1880 hanging, and film adaptations. The episode closes with calls for listener stories and website/social info.

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode as a sweet pick from the Selects series, then the hosts open the show with a brief aborted first take and banter about a Billy Joel song.

segments.title: Elderly couples who die together
segments.summary: Hosts describe a 2010 Milwaukee case in which Daniel and Kitty Goot died by helium asphyxiation in their garage in an apparent suicide pact after fifty-three years of marriage. They frame this as a broader pattern of elderly suicide pacts among long-married couples.

segments.title: Introducing broken heart syndrome
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the idea of dying from a broken heart, noting that the phrase is figurative but that medical evidence suggests emotional stress can injure the heart. They describe Dorothy Lee, who had chest pains after her husband died suddenly.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A message break from the show.

segments.title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy and its discovery
segments.summary: The hosts explain takotsubo cardiomyopathy, named after the Japanese octopus pot, first identified in Japan in the early 1990s among five heart patients with no blocked arteries. The condition causes the left ventricle to balloon, and stress or grief is suspected as a trigger.

segments.title: Studies on spousal death and mortality
segments.summary: The hosts cite a Finnish study of couples showing elevated death risk for a surviving spouse after a sudden death, and a Scotland and Israel study showing a mortality surge in the first six months of bereavement. They discuss possible explanations, including health, economics, and loss of support. They also describe brain imaging showing that heartache and physical pain light up similar neural pathways, and how adrenaline can slow the heart.

segments.title: Johns Hopkins findings and gender differences
segments.summary: The hosts describe a Johns Hopkins study finding very high adrenaline levels in broken heart patients, and note that most reported cases are women, especially women over 55. They discuss possible reasons, including post-menopausal hormones, and the ongoing debate over whether grief truly causes the condition.

segments.title: Listener mail: Ned Kelly
segments.summary: A listener from Australia writes about Ned Kelly, the Australian bushranger and national hero, who killed three policemen and survived a siege at Glenrowan in homemade armor before being hanged in 1880. The hosts discuss film adaptations and call for listener stories about couples or pets dying together.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listener stories and direct listeners to social media, email, and the website for more information.
